title: Maryland Civics & Government (10th Grade)
description: Maryland Civics & Government (10th Grade) practice - 100 questions

questions.question: At a town meeting in Chestertown, residents vote to replace their town council after a budget dispute, and a student asks why officials must accept the result instead of simply staying in office. Which founding idea is at work?
questions.correctAnswer: Popular sovereignty: governing power belongs to the people, who delegate it to officials through elections
distractors: Rule by divine right: officials hold power permanently once chosen
Judicial supremacy: courts decide which officials may remain in office
Unitary authority: a central office may ignore local election results
questions.explanation: Popular sovereignty means the people are the source of all governing authority. Officials exercise borrowed power, and elections are how citizens grant, renew, or withdraw that power.
questions.memoryHook: Officeholders are borrowers; the people own the power.

questions.question: A federal agency director is subpoenaed by a court, appears, testifies truthfully, and later pays a personal tax penalty the IRS assessed against her, with no special exemption. A commentator calls it an ordinary but important sight. Which principle does it show?
questions.correctAnswer: The rule of law: legal rules apply to government officials as well as to private citizens
distractors: Executive privilege: senior officials are exempt from ordinary legal duties
Civil supremacy: agency staff may choose which court orders to follow
Official immunity: holding office shields a person from personal taxes
questions.explanation: The rule of law means no one is above the law, including the people who administer it. When officials obey subpoenas and pay penalties like anyone else, legal status does not override legal rules.
questions.memoryHook: A title is not a shield against the law.

questions.question: A reading group in Frederick studies a 1689 to 1776 line of thought: people are born with rights no ruler grants, they form governments to protect those rights, and a government that destroys them loses its claim to obedience. Which thinker anchors this line?
questions.correctAnswer: John Locke, whose ideas of natural rights and consent deeply influenced the Declaration of Independence
distractors: Thomas Hobbes, who argued subjects owe absolute obedience to a sovereign
Baron de Montesquieu, who wrote mainly about separating government powers
James Madison, who wrote mainly about extending the sphere of a republic
questions.explanation: Locke taught that life, liberty, and property are natural rights held before government exists, and that legitimate government rests on consent. Jefferson's Declaration echoes that framework closely.
questions.memoryHook: Locke: rights are born with you, not handed to you.

questions.question: In a Hagerstown classroom, students highlight a 1776 passage listing charge after charge against a king: imposing taxes without consent, cutting off trade, and keeping standing armies in peacetime. What is the purpose of that long list inside its document?
questions.correctAnswer: To present evidence of repeated abuses justifying the colonies' separation from Britain
distractors: To propose the committee structure of a future national legislature
To set the tax schedule the new United States would collect
To offer the king terms for remaining inside the British Empire
questions.explanation: The grievance list in the Declaration of Independence is the evidentiary core of the document. It was written to show a candid world that separation followed a long train of abuses, not a sudden impulse.
questions.memoryHook: The grievances are the evidence, not decoration.

questions.question: A newly elected mayor in Salisbury tells reporters: my authority this morning comes from the same place it will come from in four years, and it can be withdrawn then. Which phrase from 1776 captures her meaning?
questions.correctAnswer: The consent of the governed
distractors: The mandate of incumbency
The divine right of kings
The supremacy of the executive
questions.explanation: The Declaration of Independence holds that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed. Consent is not permanent; it is renewed or withdrawn through later elections.
questions.memoryHook: Consent is a lease, renewed at each election.

questions.question: In 1787 a delegate complains that the national Congress can only request money from the states, cannot regulate trade between them, and watches states print rival currencies. Which governing plan created those weaknesses?
questions.correctAnswer: The Articles of Confederation, which reserved sovereignty to the states and denied Congress taxing and enforcement powers
distractors: The Constitution of 1787, which authorized Congress to tax individuals directly
The Bill of Rights, which restricted a Congress the states had empowered
The Northwest Ordinance, which governed relations among the original states
questions.explanation: Under the Articles of Confederation, Congress depended on state requisitions it could not enforce and lacked power over interstate commerce. Those structural failures led directly to the Philadelphia Convention.
questions.memoryHook: A government that can only ask cannot govern.

questions.question: Convention delegates in 1787 keep citing a recent crisis: indebted farmers in Massachusetts had closed courts by force, and the Confederation could neither pay troops nor restore order quickly. Which event were they treating as proof the old system had failed?
questions.correctAnswer: Shays' Rebellion, an armed uprising that exposed the Confederation government's weakness
distractors: The Whiskey Rebellion, a tax protest suppressed by a federalized militia in 1794
The Boston Tea Party, a protest against a parliamentary tea tax in 1773
Bacon's Rebellion, a colonial Virginia uprising against a royal governor in 1676
questions.explanation: Shays' Rebellion in 1786 and 1787 showed that the Confederation could not fund a response to internal disorder. Its shock effect pushed undecided leaders toward a stronger national government.
questions.memoryHook: Shays turned a weakness on paper into a crisis in person.

questions.question: At a history museum in Baltimore, six plain panels hang in a row beside a giant first page of the Constitution, naming a more perfect union, justice, domestic tranquility, common defense, general welfare, and the blessings of liberty. The guide stresses that these panels announce goals but hand power to no one. Which part of the document do the panels reproduce?
questions.correctAnswer: The Preamble, which states the purposes of the Constitution without granting power itself
distractors: Article I, which lists the lawmaking powers of Congress
The First Amendment, which protects five fundamental freedoms
Article VII, which set the rules for ratifying the Constitution
questions.explanation: The Preamble is the Constitution's introduction and statement of purposes. Courts treat it as a guide to intent, not as an independent grant of power to any branch.
questions.memoryHook: The Preamble is the mission statement, not the toolbox.

questions.question: A seminar in College Park examines an essay arguing that trying to eliminate competing interest groups would destroy liberty itself, so the safer cure is a large republic where many groups dilute each other's influence. Which essay makes that argument?
questions.correctAnswer: Federalist No. 10, on controlling the effects of factions in an extended republic
distractors: Federalist No. 51, on ambition counteracting ambition among the branches
Federalist No. 78, on the judiciary as the least dangerous branch
Brutus No. 1, an Anti-Federalist warning about a distant consolidated government
questions.explanation: In Federalist No. 10, Madison argued that factions are rooted in human nature and liberty, so their causes cannot be removed safely. An extended republic controls their effects by multiplying competing interests.
questions.memoryHook: No. 10: more interests, less faction control.

questions.question: An architect of constitutions explains her design: give each department the constitutional means and personal motives to resist encroachment, so ambition itself guards the boundaries. Which essay is the classic statement of that design?
questions.correctAnswer: Federalist No. 51, where Madison argues that ambition must be made to counteract ambition
distractors: Federalist No. 10, where Madison argues that factions are controlled by an extended republic
Federalist No. 70, where Hamilton argues for energy in a single executive
The Anti-Federalist Letters of Cato, which opposed ratifying the Constitution
questions.explanation: Federalist No. 51 defends separation of powers joined to checks and balances. Because men are not angels, the design makes each branch's ambition a defense against the others' encroachments.
questions.memoryHook: No. 51: ambition is the guard dog of the branches.

questions.question: A Massachusetts farmer tells a delegate to his state's 1788 ratifying convention that he cannot support a national charter which, unlike his own state constitution, opens with no declaration of rights at all. He switches to yes only when leading supporters pledge that amendments supplying such a declaration will be the new government's first business. Which group's objection extracted that pledge?
questions.correctAnswer: The Anti-Federalists, whose objections led to the Bill of Rights
distractors: The Federalists, whose published platform already contained a bill of rights
The Loyalists, whose petitions produced a charter of colonial rights
The abolitionists, whose campaigns produced the Reconstruction Amendments
questions.explanation: Anti-Federalists attacked the Constitution for creating a powerful national government with no bill of rights. Federalist promises of amendments helped secure ratification, and the first Congress proposed the Bill of Rights in 1789.
questions.memoryHook: The Bill of Rights was a promise made to win ratification.

questions.question: A proposed constitutional change clears two-thirds of both houses of Congress. A first-year staffer asks whether a meeting of three-fourths of the state legislatures could also have launched a change, and what that alternative route is. Under Article V, what is it?
questions.correctAnswer: A national convention called by Congress on the application of two-thirds of the state legislatures
distractors: A presidential commission whose proposals take effect after a national referendum
A Supreme Court conference whose proposals take effect after Senate confirmation
A governors' summit whose proposals take effect after majority state approval
questions.explanation: Article V provides two proposal routes: two-thirds of both houses of Congress, or a convention Congress must call when two-thirds of state legislatures apply. Either route's proposals require ratification by three-fourths of the states.
questions.memoryHook: Two doors into Article V; ratification guards both.

questions.question: A state inspector orders freight railroads to fit a specific brake system at its border crossings, but a valid federal rail safety rule for interstate lines requires different equipment on the same trains, and a railroad cannot obey both at once. Which clause tells a court which rule must give way?
questions.correctAnswer: The Supremacy Clause, which makes valid federal law prevail over conflicting state law
distractors: The Tenth Amendment, which makes state law prevail within state waters
The Full Faith and Credit Clause, which lets each state choose its own rule
The Privileges and Immunities Clause, which lets the older rule prevail
questions.explanation: Article VI makes the Constitution, federal statutes, and treaties the supreme law of the land. When a valid federal rule genuinely conflicts with a state rule, the federal rule controls.
questions.memoryHook: In a true conflict, valid federal law is supreme.

questions.question: A display in a Silver Spring library shows two columns of real powers: the nation declares war and coins money, while states run schools and license drivers, and both may tax. Which constitutional arrangement does the display describe?
questions.correctAnswer: Federalism, the division of governing power between national and state governments
distractors: A unitary system, where one central government holds all governing power
A confederation, where a central office only advises sovereign member states
Direct democracy, where citizens vote personally on every public decision
questions.explanation: Federalism splits authority between two levels of government, each with genuine powers of its own. Delegated, reserved, and concurrent powers are the working pieces of that arrangement.
questions.memoryHook: Two levels of government, each holding real power.

questions.question: A county sheriff in Garrett County enforces state criminal law, runs the local side of policing, and answers to state courts, all without any grant of that authority from Washington. Which amendment explains where that state authority rests?
questions.correctAnswer: The Tenth Amendment, which reserves undelegated powers to the states or to the people
distractors: Article I, which delegates ordinary police power to Congress
The Necessary and Proper Clause, which lends federal power to counties
The Fourteenth Amendment, which assigns policing to the national government
questions.explanation: Powers not delegated to the United States and not prohibited to the states are reserved to the states or the people. Ordinary criminal law enforcement is the classic exercise of that reserved state police power.
questions.memoryHook: What was never handed over stayed with the states.

questions.question: A student lists powers the national government holds because the Constitution names them: declare war, coin money, establish post offices, and regulate commerce among the states. What is the correct label for powers of this kind?
questions.correctAnswer: Enumerated, or delegated, powers expressly granted to the national government
distractors: Reserved powers retained by the states under the Tenth Amendment
Concurrent powers exercised jointly by states and counties
Implied powers inferred from the structure of state constitutions
questions.explanation: Enumerated powers are the powers the Constitution expressly lists for the national government, mostly in Article I, Section 8. Naming them in the text is what makes them delegated rather than reserved.
questions.memoryHook: Enumerated means written on the national list.

questions.question: Maryland taxes the Baltimore branch of a federally chartered bank, arguing that states may tax anything inside their borders. In 1819 the Supreme Court strikes the tax down and upholds Congress's power to charter the bank in the first place. Which case and clause pairing is this?
questions.correctAnswer: McCulloch v. Maryland, resting on the Necessary and Proper Clause and the Supremacy Clause
distractors: Marbury v. Madison, resting on the Appointments Clause and Article III
Gibbons v. Ogden, resting on the Treaty Clause and the Full Faith and Credit Clause
Dred Scott v. Sandford, resting on the Fugitive Slave Clause and the Tenth Amendment
questions.explanation: McCulloch v. Maryland held that chartering a bank was a legitimate means of executing Congress's fiscal powers, and that a state tax on a federal instrument violated supremacy: the power to tax involves the power to destroy.
questions.memoryHook: Maryland lost, and implied powers won a landmark.

questions.question: A mock government in a Bowie classroom assigns one team to write rules, a second team to run the school store under them, and a third to settle arguments about what the rules mean, and forbids any team from doing another team's work. Which principle is being modeled?
questions.correctAnswer: Separation of powers
distractors: Federalism
Judicial review
Popular sovereignty
questions.explanation: Separation of powers divides government's three jobs - making, enforcing, and interpreting law - among distinct branches, so no single body controls the whole process. Montesquieu supplied the theory; the Framers built it into three separate articles. It differs from checks and balances, which is how the separated branches push back on each other.
questions.memoryHook: Three jobs, deliberately in different hands.

questions.question: Within a single year, the Senate refuses to confirm a cabinet nominee, the President vetoes a defense bill, and Congress then falls short of overriding him. An instructor labels the whole pattern with one phrase. Which phrase fits best?
questions.correctAnswer: Checks and balances, because each branch used a constitutional tool to restrain another
distractors: Separation of powers, because the branches acted without interacting at all
Federalism, because authority moved between national and state governments
Judicial review, because a court resolved the disagreement between branches
questions.explanation: Confirmation, veto, and override are checks: tools one branch holds against another. Where separation of powers divides the jobs, checks and balances let the branches actively limit each other.
questions.memoryHook: A check is a branch pushing back with a tool.

questions.question: A dismissed federal officeholder in 1803 asks the Supreme Court to order his commission delivered, but the Court instead declares the very statute authorizing his request unconstitutional. Which landmark power did the Court claim in Marbury v. Madison?
questions.correctAnswer: Judicial review, the power to declare acts of government unconstitutional
distractors: Judicial appointment, the power of courts to select their own members
Judicial override, the power of courts to enact replacement statutes
Judicial pardon, the power of courts to forgive federal offenses
questions.explanation: Marbury v. Madison established judicial review: when a statute conflicts with the Constitution, courts must follow the Constitution. Chief Justice Marshall grounded the power in the judicial duty to say what the law is.
questions.memoryHook: Marbury: courts measure laws against the Constitution.

questions.question: Congress sets safety and emissions rules for trucks hauling produce from the Eastern Shore to markets in three other states, and a carrier argues Congress may regulate only goods already crossing a border, not the hauling business itself. Which clause gives Congress the stronger argument?
questions.correctAnswer: The Commerce Clause, which empowers Congress to regulate commerce among the states
distractors: The Taxing Clause, which empowers Congress to collect duties on exports
The Patent Clause, which empowers Congress to secure inventors' rights
The Militia Clause, which empowers Congress to organize state militias
questions.explanation: The Commerce Clause has been read to reach economic activity that substantially affects interstate commerce, including the business of interstate hauling itself. Regulation of channels and instrumentalities of interstate commerce is core congressional territory.
questions.memoryHook: Interstate business is commerce Congress can reach.

questions.question: A couple marries in Pennsylvania, wins a civil judgment in a Virginia court, and later moves to Maryland, where officials in each case must honor the marriage record and the judgment rather than retry them. Which clause requires that interstate respect?
questions.correctAnswer: The Full Faith and Credit Clause of Article IV
distractors: The Privileges or Immunities Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment
The Contracts Clause of Article I, Section 10
The Extradition Clause of Article IV, Section 2
questions.explanation: Article IV's Full Faith and Credit Clause requires states to recognize the public acts, records, and judicial proceedings of other states. It is what makes marriages, licenses, and judgments portable across state lines.
questions.memoryHook: Judgments and records travel with you across states.

questions.question: A nurse in Silver Spring pays a federal income tax on her wages in April and a Maryland income tax on the same earnings, and both of those governments also borrow money and run court systems of their own. Which category of power is she bumping into from three directions at once?
questions.correctAnswer: Concurrent powers, authority shared by the national and state governments
distractors: Enumerated powers, authority held by the national government alone
Reserved powers, authority held by the states entirely alone
Denied powers, authority the Constitution forbids to both levels
questions.explanation: Concurrent powers, such as taxing, borrowing, building roads, and maintaining courts, are exercised by both levels of government simultaneously. Sharing the power is the defining feature of the category.
questions.memoryHook: Concurrent means both levels hold the same tool.

questions.question: A civics exam gives two scenarios: Congress creates a federal bank though banking is never mentioned in the Constitution, and a state operates public schools though education is never mentioned either. Which pairing correctly sorts the two powers?
questions.correctAnswer: The bank rests on implied powers under the Necessary and Proper Clause; the schools rest on reserved powers under the Tenth Amendment
distractors: The bank is a reserved state power under the Tenth Amendment, while schooling is an enumerated power listed in Article I
Both powers are concurrent, held jointly by the national and state governments
Both powers are among those the Bill of Rights denies to every level of government
questions.explanation: Implied powers let Congress choose means for carrying out enumerated ends, as McCulloch confirmed for the national bank. Education, never delegated, remains a reserved state power under the Tenth Amendment.
questions.memoryHook: Implied stretches federal means; reserved keeps the rest.

questions.question: A pastor in Cumberland is fined for preaching without a permit, a newspaper in the same town is shut for criticizing the governor, and a peaceful march is banned outright. A lawyer says a single amendment covers all three disputes. Which one?
questions.correctAnswer: The First Amendment, which protects religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition
distractors: The Second Amendment, which protects the keeping and bearing of arms
The Fourth Amendment, which protects against unreasonable searches
The Seventh Amendment, which protects jury trials in civil cases
questions.explanation: The First Amendment bundles five freedoms: religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition. A sermon, a newspaper, and a march fall under three different freedoms inside that one amendment.
questions.memoryHook: Five freedoms live in the First Amendment.

questions.question: A public school opens each morning with a prayer composed by the state and read aloud by teachers, and a student who objects is told to stand in the hall. Which First Amendment doctrine is at the center of her challenge?
questions.correctAnswer: The Establishment Clause: government may not sponsor or establish religious practice in its own institutions
distractors: The Free Exercise Clause: government may not let students leave a sponsored prayer
The Speech Clause: government may not compose spoken texts of any kind
The Press Clause: government may not publish religious material in schools
questions.explanation: School-sponsored prayer makes the state itself the author and sponsor of a religious exercise, which the Establishment Clause forbids. Engel v. Vitale struck down exactly that arrangement in 1962.
questions.memoryHook: The state cannot write the morning prayer.

questions.question: After a court verdict he bitterly opposes, a man stands on the courthouse steps in Frederick, sets fire to a flag he brought with him, and is arrested under a law punishing anyone who treats the national flag with contempt. His defense is that the act itself was his message. Under Texas v. Johnson, how does the case come out?
questions.correctAnswer: The conviction fails: flag burning as political expression is symbolic speech protected by the First Amendment
distractors: The conviction stands: the flag is property of the government and cannot be expressive material
The conviction stands: offensive expression loses protection when crowds witness it
The conviction fails only if the flag was privately owned by someone else
questions.explanation: Texas v. Johnson (1989) held that burning the flag to express an idea is symbolic speech, and government may not ban it to protect the flag as a symbol. Offensiveness alone does not remove First Amendment protection.
questions.memoryHook: Johnson: even burning a symbol can be speech.

questions.question: Officers who suspect a College Park renter of fraud enter his home while he is at work, without a warrant, consent, or any emergency, and copy papers from his desk to build their case. Which protection does his lawyer invoke first?
questions.correctAnswer: The Fourth Amendment, which requires searches of a home to be reasonable and normally supported by a warrant based on probable cause
distractors: The First Amendment, which protects the papers as a form of press activity
The Fifth Amendment, which protects owners from testifying about their property
The Eighth Amendment, which protects homes from excessive official entry fees
questions.explanation: The home sits at the core of the Fourth Amendment. A warrantless, nonconsensual entry to gather evidence, with no emergency exception, is the textbook unreasonable search the amendment prohibits.
questions.memoryHook: The front door is where the Fourth Amendment is strongest.

questions.question: Detectives arrest a man at a bus terminal, book him, and then question him for hours in a small precinct room, never mentioning any right to silence or to a lawyer, until he confesses. His attorney moves to keep the confession out of his trial. What is the strongest argument for the motion?
questions.correctAnswer: Miranda warnings were required before custodial interrogation, and without them the confession is presumptively compelled under the Fifth Amendment
distractors: The Sixth Amendment was violated because no jury was present during the interrogation
The Seventh Amendment was violated because no jury heard the interrogation
The Tenth Amendment was violated because state officers conducted the questioning
questions.explanation: Miranda v. Arizona requires warnings about silence and counsel before custodial interrogation so the Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination is protected in the station house. Unwarned custodial statements are generally excluded.
questions.memoryHook: No warnings in custody means the words stay out.

questions.question: A defendant too poor to hire a lawyer is tried for a serious felony in a state court, convicted, and argues on appeal that the trial was fundamentally unfair without counsel. Which precedent supports him, and through which amendment does it reach the states?
questions.correctAnswer: Gideon v. Wainwright: the Sixth Amendment right to counsel applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment
distractors: Mapp v. Ohio: the Fourth Amendment exclusionary rule applies to the states through the First Amendment
Brown v. Board of Education: the Equal Protection Clause supplies counsel in felony trials
Baker v. Carr: the Guarantee Clause requires states to fund defense attorneys
questions.explanation: Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) held that counsel is a fundamental right essential to a fair trial. The Sixth Amendment obligation was applied to state courts through the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause.
questions.memoryHook: Gideon: a fair trial needs a lawyer you can actually get.

questions.question: A judge sets bail for a first-time, nonviolent defendant at a figure many times his family's total savings, openly saying the amount is meant to punish him before trial. Which amendment gives him his challenge?
questions.correctAnswer: The Eighth Amendment, which prohibits excessive bail
distractors: The Fourth Amendment, which prohibits unreasonable pretrial conditions
The Sixth Amendment, which prohibits delays before a speedy trial
The Ninth Amendment, which prohibits penalties not listed in statutes
questions.explanation: The Eighth Amendment bars excessive bail, and bail's legitimate purpose is ensuring appearance and safety, not punishment before conviction. A figure set to punish rather than to secure appearance is constitutionally excessive.
questions.memoryHook: Bail secures appearance; it is not pre-trial punishment.

questions.question: A 2008 case reaches the Supreme Court after a city bans nearly all handgun possession in the home, and a resident argues the ban violates a personal constitutional right. Which holding resolved the case?
questions.correctAnswer: District of Columbia v. Heller: the Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep a handgun in the home for self-defense
distractors: United States v. Miller: the Second Amendment protects only weapons issued by state militias
McDonald v. Chicago: the Second Amendment was first created as a right in 2010
Caetano v. Massachusetts: the Second Amendment covers only weapons existing in 1791
questions.explanation: Heller held that the Second Amendment protects an individual right, centered on self-defense in the home, and struck down the near-total handgun ban. McDonald later applied that right against the states.
questions.memoryHook: Heller: an individual right, strongest in the home.

questions.question: In a debate over a proposed law, a legislator insists the people's rights are a finished inventory: any freedom not named among the first eight amendments was surrendered when the list was ratified. Which amendment was written precisely to refute that reading?
questions.correctAnswer: The Ninth Amendment, which provides that listing certain rights does not deny others retained by the people
distractors: The Third Amendment, which provides that unlisted housing rights remain with homeowners
The Seventh Amendment, which provides that unlisted civil rights remain with juries
The Eleventh Amendment, which provides that unlisted rights remain with state courts
questions.explanation: The Ninth Amendment was added to answer the fear that a written list would be read as complete. Rights not enumerated in the Constitution are retained by the people rather than surrendered by omission.
questions.memoryHook: The list is a floor for rights, not a ceiling.

questions.question: A state in 1920 argues the Bill of Rights limits only the federal government, so it may ignore a freedom the First Amendment names. A lawyer answers that most of those protections now bind states too. Which doctrine, and which clause, carried them there?
questions.correctAnswer: Selective incorporation, applying most Bill of Rights protections to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause
distractors: Reverse incorporation, applying state constitutions to the federal government through Article VI
Total federalism, applying every federal rule to the states through the Tenth Amendment
Privileges incorporation, applying the Bill of Rights through the Commerce Clause
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court has incorporated most Bill of Rights guarantees against the states one by one, using the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause. The process is called selective incorporation because it proceeded right by right, case by case.
questions.memoryHook: The Fourteenth Amendment carried most rights to the states.

questions.question: Parents in the 1950s challenge a system assigning children to separate public schools by race, even where the buildings and books are comparable, arguing the separation itself brands their children as inferior. Which ruling vindicated that argument?
questions.correctAnswer: Brown v. Board of Education, holding that separate educational facilities are inherently unequal under the Equal Protection Clause
distractors: Plessy v. Ferguson, holding that separate facilities satisfy equality if they are comparable
Dred Scott v. Sandford, holding that public schools fall outside constitutional review
Regents v. Bakke, holding that school assignment by race is a permissible remedy
questions.explanation: Brown (1954) held that separating children in public education solely by race generates a feeling of inferiority that retards educational and mental development. Separate facilities in that setting are inherently unequal, whatever their physical quality.
questions.memoryHook: Brown: separation itself was the inequality.

questions.question: After the Civil War, a registrar tries to block a Black citizen from voting by pointing to his grandfather's enslavement. Which Reconstruction amendment directly forbids denying the vote on that basis?
questions.correctAnswer: The Fifteenth Amendment, which bars denying the vote on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude
distractors: The Thirteenth Amendment, which bars literacy tests in Southern states
The Fourteenth Amendment, which bars fees at voter registration offices
The Twelfth Amendment, which bars discrimination in electoral vote counting
questions.explanation: The Fifteenth Amendment, ratified in 1870, provides that the right to vote shall not be denied on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude. Devices like grandfather clauses were built to evade exactly that text.
questions.memoryHook: Fifteenth: race is never a voting qualification.

questions.question: In August 1920, suffragists wait for word from the last state needed to ratify a constitutional change, knowing that once it lands, no state may keep women from the ballot on account of sex. Which amendment are they waiting for?
questions.correctAnswer: The Nineteenth Amendment
distractors: The Eighteenth Amendment
The Twenty-first Amendment
The Equal Rights Amendment
questions.explanation: The Nineteenth Amendment, ratified in 1920, provides that the right to vote shall not be denied or abridged on account of sex. Its ratification completed more than seventy years of organized suffrage campaigning.
questions.memoryHook: Nineteenth: sex cannot bar the ballot.

questions.question: In 1971 a patchwork frustrates everyone: a recent court ruling has let eighteen-year-olds vote for President and Congress, yet most states still bar them from state ballots, even as eighteen-year-olds are being drafted for Vietnam. Which amendment ended the patchwork by setting one national floor for voting age?
questions.correctAnswer: The Twenty-sixth Amendment, which bars denying the vote to citizens eighteen or older on account of age
distractors: The Twenty-third Amendment, which sets eighteen as the voting age in the District of Columbia
The Twenty-fourth Amendment, which sets eighteen as the age for federal jury service
The Twenty-fifth Amendment, which sets eighteen as the age for military conscription
questions.explanation: Ratified in 1971, the Twenty-sixth Amendment lowered the voting age to eighteen in all elections. Its rapid ratification was driven by the fairness argument summed up as old enough to fight, old enough to vote.
questions.memoryHook: Twenty-sixth: eighteen votes, in every election.

questions.question: A chart in a civics textbook shows one chamber whose seats are divided among the states by population after each census, and a second chamber where Delaware and California hold exactly the same number of seats. Which two chambers fill the chart?
questions.correctAnswer: The House of Representatives, apportioned by population, and the Senate, with two members per state
distractors: The House of Commons, apportioned by counties, and the House of Lords, seated by inheritance
The Electoral College, apportioned by districts, and the Cabinet, seated by appointment
The General Assembly, apportioned by counties, and the Council of State, seated equally
questions.explanation: The Great Compromise joined the Virginia Plan's population-based house to the New Jersey Plan's equal-state chamber. The 435 House seats follow population; every state, large or small, elects exactly two senators.
questions.memoryHook: The House counts people; the Senate counts states.

questions.question: Only one-third of a chamber stands for election every two years, even though each member serves six years, so the body never turns over all at once. Which chamber works this way, and why was it designed so?
questions.correctAnswer: The Senate: staggered six-year terms keep an experienced, continuously sitting body while still facing voters regularly
distractors: The House: staggered six-year terms keep district experts in place between censuses
The Senate: staggered six-year terms exist so the President can appoint replacements
The House: staggered six-year terms exist so states can equalize district populations
questions.explanation: Senators serve six-year terms with one-third elected every two years. The staggered design was meant to give the Senate stability and institutional memory while keeping it accountable in regular installments.
questions.memoryHook: One-third at a time: stability with accountability.

questions.question: A twenty-six-year-old architect in Gaithersburg, a citizen for life and a Maryland resident for years, asks which federal legislative office she is old enough to seek this year and how long its term runs. What is the correct answer?
questions.correctAnswer: The House of Representatives: minimum age twenty-five, two-year terms
distractors: The Senate: minimum age twenty-five, two-year terms
The House of Representatives: minimum age thirty, six-year terms
The Senate: minimum age twenty-one, four-year terms
questions.explanation: House members must be at least twenty-five, citizens for seven years, and residents of the state they represent, and they serve two-year terms. Senators must be at least thirty and serve six-year terms.
questions.memoryHook: Twenty-five and two years: that is the House.

questions.question: A health bill passes the House, is amended in the Senate, and the two chambers must now agree on one identical text before anything else can happen. Trace the remaining steps in the correct order.
questions.correctAnswer: Conference agreement on one text, passage by both chambers, then presentation to the President to sign or veto
distractors: Presidential signature, then conference agreement, then a final Senate vote only
Supreme Court review, then passage by both chambers, then gubernatorial approval
Committee markup in the House only, then automatic enrollment as law
questions.explanation: A bill must pass both chambers in identical form before it is presented to the President. Conference committees exist to reconcile differing versions, and presentment for signature or veto comes last.
questions.memoryHook: Same text, both chambers, then the President.

questions.question: A President vetoes a popular infrastructure bill, sending it back with objections. Supporters announce they will try to enact it anyway. What exactly must they assemble, and where?
questions.correctAnswer: A two-thirds vote in each chamber of Congress to override the veto
distractors: A majority vote in the Senate and the Vice President's tie-breaking assent
A two-thirds vote of state governors at their annual conference
A majority of the Supreme Court agreeing the veto was unwise
questions.explanation: The veto override requires two-thirds of both the House and the Senate. It is deliberately harder than the majority needed to pass the bill the first time, which is why successful overrides are uncommon.
questions.memoryHook: Passing takes half; overriding takes two-thirds, twice.

questions.question: A cabinet secretary stands accused of taking gifts from a contractor her department regulates. One chamber of Congress votes out formal charges against her by simple majority, and the case then moves to the other chamber, which sits in judgment and can remove her only by an extraordinary majority. Which pairing of roles and threshold is correct?
questions.correctAnswer: The House impeaches by majority vote; the Senate tries the case and convicts only by two-thirds
distractors: The Senate impeaches by two-thirds vote; the House tries the case and convicts by majority
The House impeaches and tries the case, with the Chief Justice deciding guilt
The Attorney General impeaches; a jury of state governors convicts by two-thirds
questions.explanation: Impeachment is split: the House brings the charges, acting like a prosecutor, and the Senate sits as the trial body. Removal requires conviction by two-thirds of the Senate, a threshold no president has ever met.
questions.memoryHook: House accuses; Senate decides, by two-thirds.

questions.question: A President nominates an ambassador and a Supreme Court justice in the same week, and both nominations sit awaiting action in the same chamber. Which chamber holds that confirming power, and what is the power called?
questions.correctAnswer: The Senate, exercising its advice and consent power over appointments
distractors: The House, exercising its power of the purse over appointments
The Senate, exercising its power to originate revenue legislation
The House, exercising its advice and consent power over treaties
questions.explanation: Article II gives the President power to appoint ambassadors and judges with the advice and consent of the Senate. The House has no role in confirming presidential appointments.
questions.memoryHook: Appointments go to the Senate for consent.

questions.question: Two members argue over who may start a war: one notes the President commands the armed forces day to day, the other notes a formal declaration has come only from one branch since 1941. Which branch holds the formal power to declare war?
questions.correctAnswer: Congress, under its Article I power to declare war, while the President serves as commander in chief of forces Congress raises and funds
distractors: The President, under an implied power to declare and command wars simultaneously
The Supreme Court, under its power to review the legality of military actions
The state governors, under their command of the National Guard in wartime
questions.explanation: The Constitution splits war powers: Congress declares war, raises and funds armies, while the President commands the forces as commander in chief. That split is a deliberate check on unilateral war-making.
questions.memoryHook: Congress declares; the President commands.

questions.question: For decades a state's legislature draws districts so that a rural county with sixty thousand people elects as many state senators as an urban county with six hundred thousand, and city voters sue. Under Baker v. Carr and the cases that followed, what did the courts require?
questions.correctAnswer: Legislative districts of substantially equal population, so each vote carries roughly equal weight - one person, one vote
distractors: Districts of substantially equal land area, so each county's territory carries equal weight
Districts frozen at their 1900 boundaries, so representation stays historically stable
Districts drawn by courts in every state, replacing legislatures in all reapportionment
questions.explanation: Baker v. Carr opened apportionment to judicial review, and Reynolds v. Sims required state legislative districts of substantially equal population. The principle is that legislators represent people, not trees or acres.
questions.memoryHook: Districts count people, not acreage.

questions.question: A senator speaks for nineteen hours to delay a vote she cannot defeat outright, and the majority leader announces he will file a motion needing sixty votes to end the debate. Which Senate practice and mechanism are on display?
questions.correctAnswer: The filibuster, ended only by cloture, which requires three-fifths of the Senate - sixty votes
distractors: The hold, ended only by a unanimous consent agreement signed by the President
The filibuster, ended only by a simple majority under the chamber's regular rules
The quorum call, ended only by arrest of absent members by the Sergeant at Arms
questions.explanation: Senate rules protect extended debate, so most legislation can be filibustered. Cloture under Rule XXII takes sixty votes for most matters, which is why sixty is the working threshold for major Senate action.
questions.memoryHook: In the Senate, sixty is the magic number.

questions.question: A civics quiz asks for the full set of basics for one office: natural-born citizen, at least thirty-five years old, fourteen years a resident, chosen through the Electoral College for a four-year term, and serving as chief executive and commander in chief. Which office fits every clue?
questions.correctAnswer: President of the United States
distractors: Vice President of the United States, chosen separately by the Senate
Chief Justice of the United States, chosen by the Electoral College
Speaker of the House, chosen statewide by the Electoral College
questions.explanation: Article II sets those exact qualifications for the presidency, and the Twelfth Amendment electoral process selects the officeholder for a four-year term. The Twenty-second Amendment later capped service at two elected terms.
questions.memoryHook: Thirty-five, natural-born, fourteen years: President.

questions.question: On election night, Candidate A finishes second in the nationwide popular tally, yet the states A carried are worth 290 electoral votes; Candidate B won more individual ballots but states worth only 248. Who is elected President, and by what measure?
questions.correctAnswer: Candidate A: the Electoral College decides, and 270 of its 538 votes are required to win
distractors: The popular-vote winner: electoral votes are advisory once a margin exceeds one million
Neither: the House picks freely whenever the popular and electoral votes disagree
Candidate B, but only after the Supreme Court certifies the popular vote totals
questions.explanation: Presidents are chosen by electors, not by the national popular total. A majority of the 538 electoral votes - 270 - is the constitutional finish line, whatever the popular margin.
questions.memoryHook: Two hundred seventy is the only finish line.

questions.question: During a wartime labor dispute, a President orders the government to seize privately owned steel mills and run them to keep production going, although no statute authorizes the seizure and Congress has declined to grant that power. The Supreme Court strikes the order down. What limit on presidential action does the ruling illustrate?
questions.correctAnswer: An executive order cannot override or rewrite a statute; it must rest on authority from the Constitution or Congress
distractors: An executive order expires automatically unless the Senate ratifies it within thirty days
An executive order is valid only when it agrees with the President's campaign platform
An executive order cannot be reviewed by any court once it is published
questions.explanation: Executive orders and directives carry force only when they implement power the President actually holds, from Article II or a congressional delegation; in Youngstown Sheet and Tube v. Sawyer the Court voided a seizure no statute authorized. Presidential direction operates within the law, not above it.
questions.memoryHook: An order steers the law; it cannot rewrite it.

questions.question: A former senator's federal bribery conviction is barely a week old when the President issues a document forgiving the offense completely, wiping out the prison term before the appeals process has even run, and legal analysts note that Congress possesses no mechanism to undo the act. Which presidential power is this?
questions.correctAnswer: The pardon power: the President may grant pardons for offenses against the United States, except in impeachment cases
distractors: The commutation power of Congress: legislators may forgive federal sentences by resolution
The clemency power of the Supreme Court: justices may forgive sentences on appeal
The amnesty power of state governors: governors may forgive any federal sentence
questions.explanation: Article II gives the President power to grant reprieves and pardons for federal offenses, with impeachment as the sole stated exception. The power does not reach state convictions, which belong to governors or state boards.
questions.memoryHook: Federal pardon: one signature, no override.

questions.question: A President negotiates a trade agreement, commands naval forces in a crisis, and delivers an annual address, all in one month. Which single description covers the office doing the first of those jobs?
questions.correctAnswer: Chief diplomat: the President negotiates treaties and agreements, with treaties requiring Senate consent by two-thirds
distractors: Chief legislator: the President enacts trade law directly by proclamation
Chief justice: the President reviews the legality of foreign agreements
Chief administrator of Congress: the President sets both chambers' agendas
questions.explanation: As chief diplomat the President speaks for the nation abroad and negotiates its agreements. Formal treaties, however, take effect only with the consent of two-thirds of the Senate, a standing legislative check on diplomacy.
questions.memoryHook: The President negotiates; treaties still need the Senate.

questions.question: A new administration fills fifteen department head positions - State, Treasury, Defense, and others - each needing Senate confirmation, and those officials then run the daily operations of the executive branch. What is this group collectively called?
questions.correctAnswer: The Cabinet, the President's chief advisory body made up of executive department heads
distractors: The Joint Chiefs, the President's military council inside the Pentagon
The Federal Reserve Board, the President's council on monetary policy
The Executive Council, the body that confirms its own members' appointments
questions.explanation: The Cabinet consists of the heads of the fifteen executive departments, appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate. It advises the President, but its members' real work is administering their departments.
questions.memoryHook: Fifteen departments, one advisory table.

questions.question: The Vice President and a majority of the Cabinet deliver a written declaration that the President is unable to serve. The President answers Congress in writing that no inability exists; within four days the Vice President and Cabinet renew their declaration, and a constitutional decision now lands in Congress. Which amendment governs, and what must Congress find to keep the Vice President acting as President?
questions.correctAnswer: The Twenty-fifth Amendment: if the dispute continues, two-thirds of both houses must find the President unable, or the President resumes the powers of the office
distractors: The Twentieth Amendment: a simple majority of the House alone settles the dispute
The Twenty-second Amendment: the Supreme Court settles the dispute by majority vote
The Twelfth Amendment: a majority of state delegations in the Senate settles the dispute
questions.explanation: Section 4 of the Twenty-fifth Amendment lets the Vice President and a Cabinet majority declare inability, but a contesting President forces Congress to decide within twenty-one days. Keeping the Vice President in the acting role takes two-thirds of both houses.
questions.memoryHook: Disputed inability ends in a two-thirds decision.

questions.question: Congress passes a bill and adjourns within ten days; the President simply holds the bill unsigned, and it dies without any veto message or override vote. What is this outcome called, and why can Congress not respond to it?
questions.correctAnswer: A pocket veto: when Congress has adjourned, an unsigned bill cannot be returned, so there is nothing to override
distractors: A line-item veto: the President struck the bill's spending items individually
A regular veto: the bill returns automatically for an override vote next session
A legislative veto: Congress cancelled its own bill by adjourning early
questions.explanation: If Congress adjourns within the ten-day presentment window and the President takes no action, the bill fails by pocket veto. Because the bill was never formally returned, there is no veto for Congress to override.
questions.memoryHook: No return, no override: that is the pocket veto.

questions.question: An appeal travels from a federal trial court to a circuit court and finally to a court of nine justices who choose most of their cases and whose rulings bind every other court in the country. Which level has the case reached, and what kind of jurisdiction is it mostly exercising?
questions.correctAnswer: The Supreme Court of the United States, exercising appellate jurisdiction, largely through discretionary writs of certiorari
distractors: The Supreme Court of the United States, exercising original jurisdiction over all appeals
A federal district court, exercising appellate jurisdiction over the circuit courts
The Senate Judiciary Committee, exercising appellate jurisdiction over federal trials
questions.explanation: The federal ladder runs district courts, circuit courts of appeals, then the Supreme Court. Nearly everything the Supreme Court hears arrives on appeal, and it selects most of those cases by granting certiorari; its original jurisdiction is narrow, covering cases like disputes between states.
questions.memoryHook: Trial, appeal, then a court that mostly chooses.

questions.question: A federal judge rules against the administration that appointed her, remarking that she can afford to follow the law where it leads because neither her salary nor her seat depends on pleasing anyone in office. Which design feature gives her that freedom?
questions.correctAnswer: Life tenure during good behavior, with a salary that cannot be reduced while in office
distractors: Election to a ten-year term, with salary set annually by the President
Appointment at the pleasure of the Senate, with recall by majority vote
Rotation among districts every four years, with salary set by state legislatures
questions.explanation: Article III judges hold office during good behavior - effectively for life - and their compensation cannot be diminished. Federalist No. 78 defended both protections as essential to an independent judiciary.
questions.memoryHook: A judge who cannot be fired or docked can be fearless.

questions.question: A lower court judge personally believes a governing Supreme Court precedent was wrongly decided, yet rules exactly as that precedent requires and writes that her hands are tied. Which doctrine is she honoring?
questions.correctAnswer: Stare decisis: courts follow established precedent so the law stays stable and predictable
distractors: Judicial restraint: courts must agree with precedents they privately admire
Original jurisdiction: lower courts may not question any earlier ruling's logic
Certiorari: lower courts must petition before applying a precedent to a case
questions.explanation: Stare decisis, to stand by things decided, binds courts to precedent, most strictly for lower courts facing higher courts' rulings. It trades some flexibility for stability, predictability, and equal treatment across cases.
questions.memoryHook: Precedent is a promise the law keeps to itself.

questions.question: Two trials run in the same week: a burglary prosecution where the state must convince jurors beyond a reasonable doubt, and a contract suit where the plaintiff wins by showing her claim is more likely true than not. Which pair of standards is at work?
questions.correctAnswer: Beyond a reasonable doubt in the criminal case; preponderance of the evidence in the civil case
distractors: Preponderance of the evidence in both cases, since both are decided by juries
Beyond a reasonable doubt in both cases, since both end in a verdict
Probable cause in the criminal case; preponderance of the evidence in the civil case
questions.explanation: Criminal convictions demand proof beyond a reasonable doubt because liberty is at stake. Ordinary civil cases use the lower preponderance standard - more likely than not - because money, not freedom, is usually on the line.
questions.memoryHook: Freedom at stake means the highest standard.

questions.question: A city fines residents under a law so vaguely worded that no one can tell what conduct it bans, and separately argues it may punish a person without any hearing at all. A court strikes at both defects using one clause. Which distinction inside that clause covers the two defects?
questions.correctAnswer: The Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause, with a fair-warning side on clear laws and a procedural side on notice and a hearing
distractors: The Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause has a federal side for cities and a state side for counties
The First Amendment's Speech Clause has a written side for statutes and a spoken side for hearings
The Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause has a payment side for fines and a hearing side for seizures
questions.explanation: Procedural due process guarantees fair process - notice and an opportunity to be heard - before a deprivation. The fair-warning (void-for-vagueness) strand of the same clause demands that a law define the conduct it bans clearly enough for ordinary people to understand what is prohibited. The procedural side protects against deprivations of life, liberty, or property.
questions.memoryHook: Fair process, and fair limits: due process holds both.

questions.question: A President's Supreme Court nominee is grilled for two days by a Senate committee, then confirmed by the full Senate before taking the bench. Which branch performed the checking action here, and on which branch?
questions.correctAnswer: The legislative branch checked the executive branch: the Senate confirmed the President's judicial nominee
distractors: The executive branch checked the judicial branch: the President reviewed the Court's rulings
The judicial branch checked the legislative branch: the Court approved the Senate's nominee
The legislative branch checked itself: the House confirmed its own committee chair
questions.explanation: Nomination belongs to the President, but appointment requires Senate confirmation, making confirmation a legislative check on executive staffing of the judiciary. The two-day hearing is the committee stage of that check.
questions.memoryHook: One branch proposes; another must consent.

questions.question: Two organizations compete for the same voters in November: each nominates candidates, publishes a platform, raises money, and tries to win a majority so it can govern. What kind of organizations are they?
questions.correctAnswer: Political parties, whose central purpose is winning elections and controlling government
distractors: Interest groups, whose central purpose is influencing policy without holding office
Political action committees, whose central purpose is bundling member donations
Civic leagues, whose central purpose is running nonpartisan voter registration
questions.explanation: Parties are distinguished by their goal: they seek power by winning elections and placing their own people in office. Interest groups influence whoever holds office; parties try to become the officeholders.
questions.memoryHook: Parties run for the seats; groups lobby the sitters.

questions.question: In June, registered party members in Maryland choose between two candidates of their own party for a Senate nomination; in November, all voters choose between the parties' nominees for the seat itself. What are the two elections called, in order?
questions.correctAnswer: A primary election, which selects party nominees, and a general election, which selects the officeholder
distractors: A caucus of party officials, which selects party nominees, and a referendum, which selects the officeholder
A runoff between the top two primary finishers, followed by a party convention that fills the seat
An open party convention that drafts nominees, followed by a recall vote that installs them
questions.explanation: Primaries narrow each party's field to one nominee; the general election then decides who holds the office. Confusing the two is common because the same offices appear on both ballots months apart.
questions.memoryHook: Primary picks the nominee; general picks the winner.

questions.question: A Chesapeake environmental coalition never runs candidates. Instead it endorses some, grades every legislator's votes, and sends members to testify whenever a bay bill is heard. Which type of organization is it, and what is its method called?
questions.correctAnswer: An interest group, influencing policy from outside office through lobbying, endorsements, and testimony
distractors: A political party, influencing policy by nominating a full slate of candidates
A regulatory agency, influencing policy by issuing binding bay protection rules
A political action committee only, influencing policy solely by writing checks
questions.explanation: Interest groups seek to shape policy rather than to hold office themselves. Lobbying officials, testifying at hearings, and endorsing sympathetic candidates are their standard tools, protected as speech, assembly, and petition activity.
questions.memoryHook: Groups persuade the deciders; parties become them.

questions.question: A local television station spends a week investigating nursing home inspections, and within days the governor calls a press conference on the topic and legislators file three bills. Which media role is the station performing?
questions.correctAnswer: The watchdog and agenda-setting roles: exposing a problem and pushing it onto the public agenda
distractors: The gatekeeping role only: deciding which candidates may appear on the ballot
The scorekeeping role: predicting which nursing home bill will pass first
The common-carrier role: broadcasting every official statement without editing
questions.explanation: News coverage does more than report: sustained attention signals to officials and voters what matters now, which is agenda-setting. Investigating whether officials did their jobs is the press's watchdog function.
questions.memoryHook: Coverage chooses what everyone talks about next.

questions.question: A campaign polls four hundred voters chosen by random-digit dialing across a state of six million, reports a margin of error near five points, and a rival dismisses the poll because four hundred is a tiny fraction of six million. Why is the campaign's method defensible anyway?
questions.correctAnswer: A random sample can represent a large population accurately, because what matters is random selection, not population share
distractors: Any group of four hundred voters is accurate because election law certifies samples of that size
The poll is accurate because campaigns must publish their internal polling by law
Random-digit dialing guarantees every voter in the state an exactly equal voice in the results
questions.explanation: Sampling works because a random draw mirrors the population's proportions, whatever the population's size, like tasting a spoonful of well-stirred soup. Accuracy depends on randomness and sample size; the population share is nearly irrelevant.
questions.memoryHook: A random spoonful tells you about the whole pot.

questions.question: Shortly before an election, a nonprofit corporation prepares to distribute a documentary film sharply critical of a leading candidate, paid for from its general treasury and made without any contact with any campaign. Federal officials say a law banning corporate-funded election-season advocacy blocks the film. Under Citizens United v. FEC, how does the corporation's challenge fare?
questions.correctAnswer: The ban falls: independent expenditures are protected political speech, and corporate identity alone does not remove that protection
distractors: The ban stands: corporations have no speech rights in federal elections at all
The ban falls only for nonprofit corporations, never for business corporations
The ban stands because independent ads are treated as direct contributions to candidates
questions.explanation: Citizens United (2010) held that the First Amendment forbids banning independent political expenditures based on the speaker being a corporation. Direct contributions to candidates remain limitable; independent spending, uncoordinated with campaigns, is protected speech.
questions.memoryHook: Independent spending is speech; contributions are different.

questions.question: Negotiators finish a formal treaty with two allied nations, and the President announces it will bind the United States as soon as he signs. A senator corrects him on the spot. What step has the announcement skipped?
questions.correctAnswer: Ratification requires the consent of two-thirds of the Senate before the treaty binds the United States
distractors: Treaties bind the country once a majority of the House approves the final text
Treaties bind the country once the Supreme Court reviews the negotiated text
Treaties bind the country once three-fourths of the state legislatures consent
questions.explanation: Article II makes the President the negotiator but conditions treaties on two-thirds Senate consent. That supermajority requirement is why presidents often prefer executive agreements, which follow a different and lesser process.
questions.memoryHook: A treaty is not finished at the signing table.

questions.question: Congress offers states two kinds of money for the same problem: one grant arrives with detailed federal conditions on exactly how each dollar is spent, the other arrives as a broad sum for a general purpose with few strings. Which pairing names the two tools correctly?
questions.correctAnswer: Categorical grants carry specific federal conditions; block grants give states broad discretion for a general purpose
distractors: Mandates carry specific federal conditions; block grants are orders with no funding attached
Categorical grants are loans states repay; block grants are taxes states collect for Washington
Revenue sharing carries specific conditions; categorical grants give states full discretion
questions.explanation: Categorical grants fund narrowly defined purposes with conditions attached, extending federal influence into state programs. Block grants trade some federal control for state flexibility across a broad policy area.
questions.memoryHook: Strings attached, or broad freedom: name the grant.

questions.question: A student in Easton learns that Maryland's current constitution is not its first: the state governed itself under charters from 1776, 1851, and 1864 before adopting the document still in force, with amendments, today. In what year was the current Maryland Constitution adopted, and which in the sequence is it?
questions.correctAnswer: Adopted in 1867, it is Maryland's fourth constitution
distractors: Adopted in 1776, it is Maryland's first constitution, never replaced
Adopted in 1851, it is Maryland's second constitution
Adopted in 1968, it is Maryland's fifth constitution
questions.explanation: Maryland has had four constitutions: 1776, 1851, 1864, and the present one adopted in 1867. Like its predecessors, the 1867 document opens with a Declaration of Rights.
questions.memoryHook: Fourth charter, from 1867, still running Maryland.

questions.question: Before the articles of Maryland's constitution set up any office, a separate opening section lists the people's rights: free elections, freedom of speech and press, jury trial, and limits on government. What is that opening section called?
questions.correctAnswer: The Maryland Declaration of Rights, which serves as Maryland's bill of rights
distractors: The Maryland Preamble, which serves as the state's table of contents
The Articles of Confederation, which Maryland keeps as its rights list
The Maryland Code, which collects the state's criminal statutes
questions.explanation: Each Maryland constitution has opened with a Declaration of Rights, the state's own bill of rights. In the current constitution it precedes the articles that create the legislative, executive, and judicial departments.
questions.memoryHook: Maryland's rights list has its own name: the Declaration.

questions.question: A Maryland student reads the very first article of the Declaration of Rights and finds it does not list a freedom but a power: government originates from the people, exists solely for the good of the whole, and the people keep an inalienable right to alter, reform, or abolish it. Which idea is Article 1 declaring?
questions.correctAnswer: Popular sovereignty with a reserved right of the people to reform their own government
distractors: Separation of powers among three departments of state government
Federal supremacy over conflicting state laws and policies
Judicial review of statutes by the state's highest court
questions.explanation: Article 1 of the Maryland Declaration of Rights grounds all government in the people and reserves their right to alter, reform, or abolish their form of government. It is the Declaration's foundational statement, placed before every specific right.
questions.memoryHook: Article 1: the people can rebuild their government.

questions.question: Released Maryland assessment items have quoted Article 3 of the Declaration of Rights, and a student prepares for it by memorizing a paragraph about separating legislative, executive, and judicial power. Her teacher warns she has the wrong article. What does Article 3 actually say?
questions.correctAnswer: The powers not delegated to the United States, nor prohibited to the states, are reserved to the states respectively, or to the people - Maryland's echo of the Tenth Amendment
distractors: The legislative, executive, and judicial powers ought to be forever separate and distinct from each other
All government originates from the people, who may alter, reform, or abolish it at any time
Elections ought to be free and frequent, and every qualified citizen ought to have the right of suffrage
questions.explanation: Article 3 of the Maryland Declaration of Rights is a reserved-powers clause mirroring the Tenth Amendment almost word for word. Separation of powers is real in Maryland, but it is declared in Article 8, not Article 3 - the confusion the assessment items are designed to catch.
questions.memoryHook: Article 3 reserves powers; Article 8 separates them.

questions.question: A Maryland executive official announces he will also sit as a judge in cases his own department brings, citing efficiency. A delegate answers with the Declaration of Rights. Which article, and what does it command?
questions.correctAnswer: Article 8: the legislative, executive, and judicial powers ought to be forever separate and distinct
distractors: Article 3: undelegated powers are reserved to the states or to the people
Article 1: the people may alter, reform, or abolish their form of government
Article 6: officeholders are trustees of the public and accountable for their conduct
questions.explanation: Article 8 of the Maryland Declaration of Rights is one of the strongest separation-of-powers statements in any state constitution. It not only separates the three powers but expressly bars a person in one department from performing another's duties.
questions.memoryHook: Article 8 keeps Maryland's three powers in three hands.

questions.question: Article 6 of the Maryland Declaration of Rights calls everyone holding legislative or executive power a trustee of the public, accountable for their conduct, and then goes further than most rights documents dare. What does it say the people may and ought to do when government's ends are perverted and all other redress fails?
questions.correctAnswer: Reform the old government or establish a new one, rejecting the doctrine of non-resistance against arbitrary power and oppression
distractors: Petition the governor for a special session to consider their complaints
Appeal to the Supreme Court of Maryland for a writ dissolving the General Assembly
Withhold state taxes until the offending officials resign from office
questions.explanation: Article 6 pairs accountability with consequence: officials are trustees, and when government is perverted and liberty manifestly endangered with no other redress, the people may and ought to reform or replace it. It calls non-resistance to arbitrary power absurd and destructive.
questions.memoryHook: Trustees who betray the trust can be replaced.

questions.question: A Maryland judge opens a case by noting that even though the dispute is entirely inside Maryland, a provision of the United States Constitution decides part of it, and the state constitution itself says so. Which article of the Declaration of Rights makes that acknowledgment?
questions.correctAnswer: Article 2, which declares the Constitution of the United States and laws made under it to be the supreme law of the state
distractors: Article 4, which declares Maryland a free, sovereign, and independent state
Article 7, which declares that elections ought to be free and frequent
Article 12, which declares the legislature ought to be frequently convened
questions.explanation: Article 2 of the Declaration of Rights adopts federal supremacy into Maryland's own founding document, binding Maryland judges to treat the United States Constitution as the state's supreme law. It is Maryland's mirror of the federal Supremacy Clause.
questions.memoryHook: Maryland's own Article 2 bows to the United States Constitution.

questions.question: Visitors tour the State House in Annapolis and watch two chambers at work: a smaller upper chamber and a much larger lower one named for delegates rather than representatives. Give the legislature's name and the size of each chamber.
questions.correctAnswer: The General Assembly: a Senate of 47 members and a House of Delegates of 141 members
distractors: The General Assembly: a Senate of 34 members and a House of Delegates of 99 members
The State Legislature: a Senate of 47 members and a House of Representatives of 141 members
The General Court: a Senate of 40 members and a House of Delegates of 160 members
questions.explanation: Maryland's legislature is the General Assembly, and its two chambers total 188 members. The numbers are fixed in Article III of the state constitution: forty-seven senators and one hundred forty-one delegates.
questions.memoryHook: Forty-seven plus one forty-one makes Annapolis.

questions.question: A Maryland voter's ballot for state legislature looks different from her ballot for Congress: instead of one state senator and one state delegate, her district sends one senator and three delegates to Annapolis, all at the same election, all for the same term length. Which arrangement is she seeing, and how long is the term?
questions.correctAnswer: Maryland's 47 legislative districts each elect one senator and three delegates, and all serve four-year terms with no term limits
distractors: Maryland's 47 legislative districts each elect one senator and three delegates, and all serve staggered six-year terms
Maryland's eight congressional districts each elect one senator and three delegates to four-year terms
Maryland's 24 counties each elect one senator and three delegates to two-year terms
questions.explanation: Article III divides Maryland into 47 legislative districts, each returning one senator and three delegates - though several districts are split into delegate subdistricts, so voters there choose among their subdistrict's delegate seats rather than all three at once. Since the 1920s both offices have carried four-year terms, and Maryland imposes no term limits on its legislators - a direct contrast with the two-year United States House term.
questions.memoryHook: One senator, three delegates, four years, no limit.

questions.question: Two friends in Westminster compare candidacies: one, aged twenty-six, wants a House of Delegates seat; the other, aged twenty-three, wants a State Senate seat and has lived in the district for two years. Under Article III, Section 9, who is eligible, and what else must each candidate show?
questions.correctAnswer: Only the twenty-six-year-old: senators must be at least twenty-five and delegates twenty-one, with one year in Maryland and six months in the district
distractors: Both are eligible: the minimum age is twenty-one for both chambers, with one year of residence in the district and six months in the state
Only the Senate candidate: a delegate must be at least twenty-five and a senator at least twenty-one, with the same residency rules for both
Neither is eligible: both offices require age thirty, five years of residence in Maryland, and two full years living in the district
questions.explanation: Section 9 of Article III sets two age floors - twenty-five for senators, twenty-one for delegates - so the twenty-three-year-old cannot yet run for Senate. Both offices share the citizenship and residency tests: one year in Maryland and six months in the district.
questions.memoryHook: Senate waits for twenty-five; Delegates open at twenty-one.

questions.question: Annapolis runs on a distinctive rhythm: the General Assembly arrives in mid-January and must finish its regular work, including the budget, on a fixed clock that other legislatures with year-round sessions never face. How long is the regular session, when does it begin, and how can it be lengthened?
questions.correctAnswer: Ninety consecutive days beginning the second Wednesday in January; it may be extended up to thirty more days by a three-fifths vote of each house
distractors: Sixty consecutive days beginning the first Monday in February; it may be extended indefinitely by the governor
Ninety consecutive days beginning the second Wednesday in January; it may be extended only by a constitutional amendment
One hundred eighty days beginning the first Wednesday in January; it may be extended by majority vote of the Senate alone
questions.explanation: Article III limits regular sessions to ninety days from the second Wednesday in January. A three-fifths vote in each house can add up to thirty days, and the governor may call special sessions, which are themselves capped at thirty days.
questions.memoryHook: Ninety days from mid-January: Annapolis works fast.

questions.question: A Maryland governor vetoes a tax bill, and the General Assembly's leaders calmly note that overriding him is easier in Annapolis than overriding a president is in Washington. What vote does Maryland require, and how does it compare?
questions.correctAnswer: Three-fifths of each house in Maryland, a lower bar than the two-thirds of each house Congress needs
distractors: A majority of each house in Maryland, the same vote needed to pass the bill originally
Two-thirds of each house in Maryland, exactly the federal override standard
Three-fourths of each house in Maryland, a higher bar than the federal standard
questions.explanation: Article II, Section 17 of the Maryland Constitution lets the General Assembly override by three-fifths of each house - twenty-nine senators and eighty-five delegates. The federal override demands two-thirds of both chambers, so Maryland's check on its governor is deliberately lighter.
questions.memoryHook: Maryland override: three-fifths beats two-thirds for ease.
