questions.question: Maryland voters find a proposed change to their state constitution on the November ballot. A civics student traces how it got there and what cannot happen to it along the way. Which account is correct?
questions.correctAnswer: The General Assembly proposed it by three-fifths of the total membership of each house, it goes to the voters for ratification, and the governor has no veto over constitutional amendments
distractors: The governor proposed it by executive order, and it takes effect unless two-thirds of the Senate objects
The General Assembly enacted it by majority vote, and the governor may veto it like any other bill
A citizen petition placed it on the ballot, and it takes effect on a majority vote of the counties
questions.explanation: Maryland constitutional amendments originate in the General Assembly and require three-fifths of the total membership of each house. They are then submitted to the voters, whose ratification - not the governor's signature - makes them law.
questions.memoryHook: Amendments: three-fifths propose, the voters decide.

questions.question: A candidate for Maryland governor is thirty-two, has lived and voted in Maryland for six years, and wins in November. An opponent argues she cannot legally serve a second consecutive victory four years later. Who is right about her eligibility and her future?
questions.correctAnswer: She is eligible now - a governor must be at least thirty and a Maryland resident and voter for five years - and she may serve at most two consecutive four-year terms
distractors: She is ineligible now - a governor must be at least thirty-five and a Maryland resident for ten years
She is eligible now, and she may serve an unlimited number of consecutive four-year terms
She is eligible now, but Maryland governors may serve only one four-year term in a lifetime
questions.explanation: Article II requires a governor to be at least thirty years old and a resident and registered voter of Maryland for the five years before election. Governors serve four-year terms and may not serve more than two of them consecutively.
questions.memoryHook: Thirty, five years in Maryland, two terms in a row.

questions.question: On a Maryland ballot, the names for governor and lieutenant governor do not appear as separate races: voters choosing a governor automatically choose the running mate listed with that candidate. What is this arrangement called, and why does it matter?
questions.correctAnswer: A joint ballot: the governor and lieutenant governor are elected as a ticket, so the two offices are never split between rival candidates
distractors: A fused ballot: the governor appoints the lieutenant governor after winning the election
A unit ballot: the lieutenant governor is elected by the Senate from the losing ticket
A paired primary: the lieutenant governor is chosen later by the governor's party convention alone
questions.explanation: Maryland elects its governor and lieutenant governor on a joint ballot, as one ticket chosen by the voters together. The arrangement guarantees the state's top two executives come from the same candidacy rather than rival camps.
questions.memoryHook: One ticket, two offices, no split at the top.

questions.question: Every January, Maryland's governor sends the General Assembly a complete budget bill - and legislators discover their editing power over it is far narrower than Congress's power over a federal budget. What exactly may the General Assembly do to the governor's executive-branch items?
questions.correctAnswer: Strike them out or reduce them, but not increase them; only the items for the legislature itself and the judiciary may be raised or lowered
distractors: Increase, reduce, or rewrite them freely, exactly as Congress treats a presidential budget
Only reduce items for the judiciary; executive items may be increased by majority vote
Nothing at all: the budget bill becomes law exactly as the governor submits it
questions.explanation: Article III, Section 52 gives Maryland one of the strongest executive budgets in the nation. For executive items the Assembly's amendment power is limited to striking or reducing; it may increase or diminish only its own and the judiciary's items, and totals may not exceed estimated revenues.
questions.memoryHook: In Maryland's budget, Annapolis can cut but not add.

questions.question: Annapolis is often called a plural executive state: a Maryland voter does not elect only a governor in November but also fills two other statewide executive offices at the ballot box, each for four years. Which two offices does the voter elect directly?
questions.correctAnswer: The comptroller, who supervises the state's fiscal affairs, and the attorney general, the state's chief legal officer
distractors: The treasurer, who keeps the state treasury, and the secretary of state, who keeps state records
The state auditor, who examines state accounts, and the superintendent of schools
The lieutenant governor separately, and the clerk of the Supreme Court of Maryland
questions.explanation: Maryland voters directly elect the comptroller and the attorney general alongside the governor, each to a four-year term. Because these officers answer to voters rather than to the governor, Maryland's executive power is genuinely shared - the essence of a plural executive.
questions.memoryHook: Voters pick the money watcher and the top lawyer too.

questions.question: A Maryland student assumes every statewide executive officer is chosen the same way, by the voters in November. Her teacher points to one major fiscal office filled in a completely different room. Which office, and how is it filled?
questions.correctAnswer: The state treasurer, chosen by a joint ballot of both houses of the General Assembly for a four-year term
distractors: The comptroller, chosen by the governor from a list supplied by the Senate
The attorney general, chosen by the justices of the Supreme Court of Maryland
The secretary of state, chosen by statewide popular vote every four years
questions.explanation: The treasurer is the exception inside Maryland's plural executive: the office that accounts for all deposits and disbursements of the state treasury is selected by joint ballot of the Senate and House of Delegates. The secretary of state, by contrast, is appointed by the governor.
questions.memoryHook: The treasurer is picked in the legislature, not at the polls.

questions.question: Three officials meet in Annapolis to approve a major state contract, sign off on a land sale, and oversee spending of bond money - and between them they hold the governor's office and the state's two great fiscal offices. What is this three-member body?
questions.correctAnswer: The Board of Public Works, composed of the governor, the comptroller, and the treasurer, which approves major state contracts, leases, and capital spending
distractors: The Board of Revenue Estimates, composed of the governor, the Senate president, and the House speaker
The Executive Council, composed of the governor, the lieutenant governor, and the attorney general
The State Board of Canvassers, composed of the comptroller, the treasurer, and the secretary of state
questions.explanation: The Board of Public Works is Maryland's highest administrative body, written into the constitution and made of exactly three officers: governor, comptroller, and treasurer. It approves capital projects, most large procurement contracts, and sales or leases of state property.
questions.memoryHook: Governor plus two fiscal officers guard the contracts.

questions.question: A state agency is sued, a county prosecutor's office needs a formal legal opinion, and a legislator asks whether a draft bill is constitutional - and in Maryland all three matters route to the same elected official's office. Which official is it, and what is the role?
questions.correctAnswer: The attorney general, Maryland's chief legal officer, who serves as legal counsel to the governor, the legislature, and state departments and represents the state in court
distractors: The comptroller, Maryland's chief fiscal officer, who audits the legal bills of state agencies
The chief justice, who issues advisory opinions to agencies and legislators on request
The secretary of state, who certifies the legality of bills before the governor signs them
questions.explanation: The attorney general is the state's top lawyer: elected by the voters for a four-year term, the office advises state government and represents Maryland in legal proceedings. It is a legal office, not a fiscal or judicial one - those belong to the comptroller and the courts.
questions.memoryHook: Legal questions all road-trip to the attorney general.

questions.question: A Rockville resident's legal problem could start in one of two trial courts on the same street, and if she loses, her case could climb through two more levels above them. How many levels make up the Maryland court system, in order from the ground up?
questions.correctAnswer: Four levels: District Court, circuit courts, the Appellate Court of Maryland, and the Supreme Court of Maryland
distractors: Three levels: District Court, circuit courts, and the Court of Appeals
Two levels: circuit courts and the Supreme Court of Maryland
Five levels: justice courts, District Court, circuit courts, the Appellate Court, and a court of last resort in Washington
questions.explanation: Maryland courts form a four-level ladder: trial in the District Court or a circuit court, appeal to the Appellate Court of Maryland, and final review in the Supreme Court of Maryland. The two appellate courts carry names they received only in December 2022.
questions.memoryHook: Four rungs: District, circuit, Appellate, Supreme.

questions.question: A lawyer trained in New York opens a 2021 Maryland case report citing the Court of Appeals and the Court of Special Appeals, then cannot find either court in a 2024 directory. What happened to them?
questions.correctAnswer: Voters approved an amendment renaming them: the Court of Appeals became the Supreme Court of Maryland, and the Court of Special Appeals became the Appellate Court of Maryland
distractors: Both courts were abolished in 2022 and their work moved to the federal courts in Baltimore, which took over all Maryland appeals that year
Both courts were merged into a single new tribunal called the Maryland High Court in 2022, with all of their judges combined on one bench
Both courts kept their names, but their judges were retitled from justices to judges in 2022 and their courts were renumbered instead
questions.explanation: Maryland's old court names confused generations of litigants, since its Court of Appeals name matches other states' intermediate courts. The 2022 amendment, ratified by voters that November, aligned Maryland's names with the national pattern the following December. The new names took effect on December 14, 2022.
questions.memoryHook: Same courts, new names, December 2022.

questions.question: Seven justices sit on Maryland's highest court, each drawn from a different appellate judicial circuit, and none of them first won the seat in a contested election against an opponent. How did they get and keep their seats?
questions.correctAnswer: The governor appoints them with Senate confirmation, and they later stand alone in a retention election for a ten-year term
distractors: The General Assembly elects them by joint ballot, and they serve single fourteen-year terms with no election
The voters elect them in contested partisan elections to six-year terms
The chief justice appoints them, and they serve until the mandatory retirement age of seventy with no election
questions.explanation: Supreme Court of Maryland justices are appointed by the governor and confirmed by the Senate, then face the voters without an opponent in a retention election. Retention wins a ten-year term, and justices must retire at age seventy. That retention vote comes at the first general election at least a year after appointment, and voters simply vote yes or no on keeping the justice.
questions.memoryHook: Appointed, confirmed, then kept or removed by yes or no.

questions.question: A felony trial with a jury, a large civil suit, and a divorce case are all heard in the same Maryland court, the one that exists in every county and in Baltimore City and also reviews decisions of the lower trial court. Which court is it, and how do its judges keep their seats?
questions.correctAnswer: The circuit court: its judges, after any initial appointment, must win contested elections against any challengers to hold fifteen-year terms
distractors: The District Court: its judges are appointed by the governor to ten-year terms with no election
The Appellate Court of Maryland: its judges stand in retention elections for ten-year terms
The orphans' court: its judges are elected to four-year terms in each county
questions.explanation: Circuit courts are Maryland's jury trial courts of general jurisdiction, one for each county and Baltimore City, and they hear appeals from the District Court. Uniquely among Maryland judges, circuit judges can be challenged by opponents in elections for their fifteen-year terms.
questions.memoryHook: Circuit judges face real opponents; others mostly do not.

questions.question: A landlord-tenant dispute and a traffic case are heard in a Maryland court where no jury will ever sit, the amounts and offenses are smaller, and the judge reached the bench without facing voters at all. Which court is this, and how are its judges chosen and kept?
questions.correctAnswer: The District Court of Maryland: its judges are appointed by the governor and confirmed by the Senate for ten-year terms, with no election or retention vote
distractors: The circuit court: its judges are elected in contested elections for fifteen-year terms
The Appellate Court of Maryland: its judges stand in retention elections for ten-year terms
A justice court: its judges are elected by the county council for four-year terms
questions.explanation: The District Court is a single statewide court that handles traffic, landlord-tenant, small civil claims, and minor criminal cases, always before a judge alone. Its judges are the only Maryland judges who never face the voters: appointment and Senate confirmation lead directly to renewable ten-year terms.
questions.memoryHook: District Court: no jury, no election, ten-year terms.

questions.question: A geography student counts Maryland's main local jurisdictions and gets twenty-four, even though the state plainly has only twenty-three counties. What explains the extra jurisdiction?
questions.correctAnswer: Baltimore City counts as the twenty-fourth: it is a city that functions as a county-level jurisdiction alongside the twenty-three counties
distractors: Maryland has a twenty-fourth county that appears only for census purposes
The District of Columbia is counted as a Maryland jurisdiction for local services
Ocean City is counted as a separate county during the summer season
questions.explanation: For most Marylanders, county government is the main local government, and the state's map of it has one famous exception built in. Baltimore City, though a municipality, has stood on a par with the counties since the Constitution of 1851, making twenty-four county-level jurisdictions in all.
questions.memoryHook: Twenty-three counties plus one city that counts as one.

questions.question: A new resident of Baltimore is confused: she pays city taxes, elects a mayor and city council, yet her neighbor insists the city is not part of any county and that Baltimore County is a different government with its seat in Towson. Which account of Baltimore's status is correct?
questions.correctAnswer: Baltimore is an independent city: it separated from Baltimore County in 1851, is not inside any county, and performs county-level functions itself
distractors: Baltimore is the county seat of Baltimore County and shares its council and executive
Baltimore is an unincorporated district administered jointly by six surrounding counties
Baltimore is a federal district governed directly by the state comptroller
questions.explanation: Baltimore separated from Baltimore County under the Constitution of 1851 and has functioned as an independent city ever since. It runs its own courts, schools, and police as a county-equivalent, entirely apart from the neighboring county that shares its name.
questions.memoryHook: The city and the county of Baltimore are strangers.

questions.question: Eleven Maryland counties, including Montgomery, Howard, and Baltimore County, govern themselves under a written local constitution of their own: voters there elect a county council to make local laws and, in most of them, a county executive to run the administration. Which form of county government is this?
questions.correctAnswer: Charter home rule, adopted by the county's voters under Article XI-A of the Maryland Constitution
distractors: Commission government, in which a board of commissioners both legislates and administers
Code home rule, in which commissioners gain some local law power without a charter
Council-manager government, in which an appointed manager holds all executive power
questions.explanation: Charter counties are Maryland's strongest form of local self-government: a voter-adopted charter works like a local constitution, creating an elected council and, in all but Dorchester and Talbot, a separate county executive. Eleven of the twenty-three counties have chosen this form.
questions.memoryHook: A charter is a county's own constitution.

questions.question: Twelve Maryland counties are still run by boards of county commissioners, but they are not all alike: in six of them the commissioners received extra power to pass local laws without asking Annapolis, while in the other six the board simply combines legislative and executive work in the traditional way. Which pairing names the two groups correctly?
questions.correctAnswer: Code home rule counties hold the added local-law power; commission counties hold the traditional combined form - and both are governed by elected boards of county commissioners, not councils
distractors: Charter counties hold the added local-law power; code home rule counties use elected councils and executives
Commission counties hold the added local-law power; charter counties use boards of commissioners
Code home rule counties elect county executives; commission counties are run by state appointees
questions.explanation: Maryland's three county forms form a ladder of self-government. Charter counties use councils under a charter; code home rule counties keep commissioners but gain broader power to enact local laws; pure commission counties keep commissioners in the traditional role, with the General Assembly passing much of their local law.
questions.memoryHook: Commissioners in both, but code counties got extra law power.

questions.question: After the General Assembly passes an unpopular law, Maryland citizens organize to put that very law on the November ballot so voters can approve or reject it - but when the same group tries to place its own brand-new proposal on the ballot the same way, lawyers tell them Maryland law offers no such route. Which pair of direct-democracy rules explains both answers?
questions.correctAnswer: Maryland has the referendum: a petition with signatures equal to three percent of the last gubernatorial vote can refer an act to the voters - but it has no statewide initiative
distractors: Maryland has the initiative: citizens may originate laws by petition - but it has no referendum, so enacted laws cannot be referred to voters
Maryland has both tools, but a referendum requires signatures from ten percent of all registered voters statewide, gathered in every county
Maryland has neither tool: only the governor may place a law on the ballot for a popular vote, and citizens have no petition route at all
questions.explanation: Article XVI of the Maryland Constitution reserves the referendum to the people, with a signature threshold of three percent of the last gubernatorial vote and a rule that no more than half the signers come from Baltimore City or any one county. Maryland is a referendum-only state: unlike states with the initiative, its citizens cannot draft a statute and petition it directly onto the ballot.
questions.memoryHook: Maryland can refer a law; it cannot initiate one.
